vignette:
She is an 80-year-old African woman who carries herself with the steady, practiced grace of someone who has spent a lifetime helping others come into the world. For most of her adult life, she has worked as a midwife, moving between homes and clinics with a calm confidence that others have long relied on. She is married and speaks often of her family as a source of meaning, though in recent years that sense of steadiness has been shaken by what happened on the road.

The accident occurs during an ordinary day that later becomes impossible to think of as ordinary. She is traveling to work, already thinking about the women she expects to see, when the vehicle suddenly loses control. In her telling, the moment arrives without warning and then seems to split into pieces: the screech of tires, the violent impact, the sensation that her body is thrown against something hard, the helpless awareness that she cannot stop what is happening. She believes she is going to die. Even now, when she describes it, she returns to the exact feeling of her heart racing with certainty that this is the end. The terror is not abstract; it is physical, immediate, and total. She is injured, stunned, and unable to make sense of how quickly the world turns dangerous.

In the days afterward, she is changed by more than pain in her body. She becomes watchful in a way that feels unfamiliar to her. A loud sound makes her jump. The sudden braking of a car, the smell of fuel, the sight of a crowded road all pull her back into the accident before she can steady herself. She starts to avoid riding in vehicles whenever she can, and when she must travel, she sits rigidly, holding herself as still as possible, scanning the road ahead with strained attention. She knows she is not the same woman who used to go from one delivery to another without hesitation. The confidence that once came so naturally now feels fragile, as if it can be broken by a single sharp noise.

Her sleep becomes light and interrupted. At night she lies awake replaying the accident, sometimes in fragments and sometimes in full scenes that seem to arrive without permission. She wakes with her heart pounding, disoriented, and has to remind herself where she is. On some nights she dreams that the crash is happening again, and she wakes frightened, gripping the sheets, unable to settle back into sleep for a long time. During the day she finds her thoughts drifting back to the event even when she is trying to focus on something simple. A conversation can suddenly disappear from her mind because a memory intrudes with such force that she has to pause and breathe before she can continue.

As a midwife, she has spent years remaining composed in moments of danger, but after the accident she notices that she has less patience for noise, urgency, and unpredictability. She still speaks tenderly about the mothers she has helped, and she still cares deeply about the work, but she approaches it differently now. She is more guarded, more easily startled, and less willing to rush. She worries about not being able to react quickly enough if something goes wrong. At times she feels ashamed by this fear, as if age and experience should have made her stronger than it does. Instead, she finds herself feeling vulnerable in ways she had not expected at this stage of life.

She is also more easily overwhelmed by sadness and tension. Her family notices that she becomes quiet after reminders of the accident, and she sometimes withdraws rather than explain what is happening inside her. She does not like to burden others, so she keeps much of the fear to herself. Yet in private she feels the weight of it constantly: the sense that danger can appear without warning, the knowledge that her body no longer feels fully under her control, the grief of losing the ease and trust she once had in the world.

Still, she continues to show the same discipline and dignity that have defined her for decades. She rises each morning, attends to her home, and tries to return to the rhythms of her life. But the accident remains close to the surface, shaping her movements, her sleep, and the way she sees the road ahead. What once was a brief moment of catastrophe has become a lasting presence in her days, one she carries with caution, fear, and a quiet determination to keep going.
